title: He Left Hyderabad With Nothing. Now He's Buying One of India's Biggest Banks for $5 Billion.
excerpt: Indian-Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa parked $1 billion in government bonds last week. His Fairfax Financial is closing in on IDBI Bank — the largest foreign investment in an Indian bank ever.
body:
Prem Watsa left Hyderabad for Canada in 1972 with almost nothing. Five decades later, the billionaire chairman of Fairfax Financial Holdings is about to buy his way back into the Indian financial system through one of the country's largest bank privatisations.

Fairfax India Holdings, the Toronto-listed vehicle Watsa set up specifically to invest in the subcontinent, quietly purchased nearly $1 billion of Indian government bonds last week — an extraordinary move that Reuters reported was designed to bring capital into the country ahead of a potential deal to acquire a majority stake in IDBI Bank.

The bond buying was concentrated and aggressive. Fairfax picked up roughly ₹6,000 crore ($634 million) of the 6.03% 2029 government security at a yield five basis points below market — a premium that signalled both urgency and deep pockets. It added another ₹600 crore of a 2027 bond and ₹2,600 crore in short-term treasury bills, according to five treasury officials who spoke to Reuters anonymously.

## A Four-Year Saga

The government and Life Insurance Corporation of India announced the sale of their combined 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank in October 2022. It was supposed to be India's signature privatisation — a $13 billion lender, rescued from a near-death spiral of bad loans in 2018, now cleaned up and ready for private ownership.

It didn't go to plan. Financial bids received from Fairfax and Emirates NBD earlier this year came in below the reserve price. The process stalled. Talks continued quietly.



> **"A source close to the discussions told Moneycontrol the deal "seems to be headed in the right direction" and could conclude by September."**


Now, according to Outlook Business citing Moneycontrol, Fairfax has returned with a revised all-cash bid of approximately ₹77 per share — a discount to the bank's market price of ₹87 but one that could still fetch roughly ₹50,000 crore ($5.3 billion) for the government and LIC combined. A source close to the discussions told Moneycontrol the deal "seems to be headed in the right direction" and could conclude by September.

## The Architecture of the Deal

If completed, IDBI Bank will become the anchor of Fairfax's entire financial services strategy in India. Watsa's plan is to fold GoDigit General Insurance, the digital-first insurer he co-founded with former Allianz CEO Kamlesh Goyal, and IIFL Capital Services into IDBI Bank as subsidiaries — creating a conglomerate that spans banking, insurance, and wealth management under a single brand.

The move also triggers a mandatory exit from CSB Bank. Fairfax acquired a 51% stake in the Kerala-based lender (then Catholic Syrian Bank) in 2018, rescuing it from collapse. Under RBI rules, a promoter cannot hold two banking licences. Fairfax has committed to divesting its now-40% CSB stake once the IDBI acquisition closes.

## Why the Bonds Matter

India recently exempted foreign investors in government bonds from capital gains tax — a change that made Fairfax's $1 billion bond purchase commercially viable. The bonds serve a dual purpose: they park capital inside India while earning a yield, and they demonstrate to regulators and the government that Fairfax is serious, liquid, and ready to close.

As a Reuters source noted, Fairfax is not a regular participant in Indian bond markets. Its previous exposure was a modest $42.6 million in government securities at the end of 2025. The hundred-fold scale-up in a single week was, by any measure, a statement.

## The Diaspora Angle

Prem Watsa's story is one of Indian emigration and return. Born into a Telugu-speaking family in Hyderabad, he arrived in Canada at 21, earned an MBA, and built Fairfax into a $30 billion insurance and investment empire. His return to India via IDBI Bank would make the largest-ever foreign direct investment in an Indian bank — and the fact that it comes from a first-generation immigrant carries symbolic weight that both New Delhi and Ottawa recognise.

The deal also arrives at a delicate moment in India-Canada relations, which have been strained by diplomatic disputes over the past two years. A multi-billion-dollar Indian-Canadian investment in India's banking sector is, among other things, a data point that economic ties can run deeper than political friction.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the privatisation signals a broader shift: India's banking sector, long dominated by lumbering state-owned giants, is opening up to global capital and management — and sometimes, the capital comes home.

*Sources: Reuters, Outlook Business, Moneycontrol, Insurance Business Magazine*
